title: PM's adviser urges multi-year Rohingya funding as BRAC study lands
excerpt: Aid cuts will not speed up repatriation, Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir said. A BRAC survey finds young Rohingya with an income are keener to go home.
content:
Short-term aid renewed year by year is "the most expensive way to manage a long crisis", Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, the Prime Minister's adviser on finance and planning, said at a BRAC policy dialogue in Dhaka on Thursday (19 November), The Business Standard reported. "Cutting support will not hasten repatriation," he said.

The dialogue, "Rohingya crisis at year ten and beyond: rethinking the response", also presented a new BRAC study on young Rohingya and host community members in Ukhiya and Teknaf.

The funding gap

Titumir said the Rohingya population has grown by 37% while international assistance has fallen by 34%. The Joint Response Plan targets 1.56 million people, 1.25 million Rohingya and about 300,000 host community members. It seeks $710 million, 25% less than last year, and was 37% underfunded when it was launched in May.

He asked donors for multi-year, development-oriented funding for education, skills, livelihoods and host communities, and named the World Bank, IMF and ADB as possible investors in Rakhine, The Daily Star reported. The Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner also called for a medium-term approach covering education and self-reliance, The Daily Star reported.

What the BRAC study found

BRAC interviewed 1,152 Rohingya and host community young people aged 15 to 35, The Daily Star reported. Among Rohingya youth with some income, 79.3% want to return to Myanmar, against 53.4% of those without income. 82.6% would return if citizenship and equal rights were guaranteed.

Almost half of young Rohingya (49.7%) neither study nor work, rising to 84.5% for young women. Among host community youth, 66.7% say their livelihoods have been damaged and 95.5% want the government to create local jobs.

Why it matters

This is a clear public signal from the government in favour of the kind of multi-year, livelihoods-focused funding that NGOs in Cox's Bazar have asked for. The BRAC data also challenges the idea that keeping refugees idle encourages return: income appears to go with a stronger wish to go home.

What to watch

Whether donors and the government agree on livelihood and skills programmes in the camps, and how the 2027 Joint Response Plan is framed.
